message.content:
SEO fixes + new blog content for /opt/nxeon (Next.js 15 App Router marketing site for "Nxeon", a VPS host). Do NOT run git. Do NOT touch prisma/schema.prisma, app/admin, app/dashboard, terminal-server/, or lib/actions-improvements. Verify with tsc + build at the end. Read app/layout.tsx first to understand the current metadata/title setup.

Two confirmed SEO bugs to fix:
1. **Doubled title suffix**: pages render like `"VPS Hosting — Nxeon · Nxeon"` because page `metadata.title` strings already contain "— Nxeon" (or "| Nxeon") AND the root layout applies a `title.template` that appends "· Nxeon". Fix cleanly so every page renders ONE suffix, e.g. `"VPS Hosting — Nxeon"`. Preferred approach: (a) in `app/layout.tsx` set `title: { default: "<the homepage title>", template: "%s — Nxeon" }`, and (b) go through every `app/(marketing)/**/page.tsx` (and other pages with metadata) and STRIP the trailing "— Nxeon" / "| Nxeon" / "· Nxeon" from their `metadata.title` so the template adds it exactly once. Homepage keeps the full default (no template). Verify a couple of pages render a single suffix after building.
2. **Identical `og:title` (and likely `og:description`) on every page**: the root layout hardcodes `openGraph.title`/`openGraph.description`, so social/share previews are the same everywhere. Fix so each page's OpenGraph title/description derive from that page's own title/description. Best: in `app/layout.tsx` set `openGraph.title` to a template object `{ default, template: "%s — Nxeon" }` (Next.js supports this) so page titles propagate to og:title; and ensure pages that set a `description` also flow it to `openGraph.description` (either per page, or rely on Next merging — verify by curling built output). The goal: `og:title` differs per page.

Also improve SEO breadth:
3. Ensure every major marketing page has a UNIQUE, keyword-rich `metadata.description` (~150–160 chars). Fix any that are missing or duplicated. Keep titles keyword-front-loaded.

New blog content:
4. Add NEW blog posts covering the recent launches so they're indexed. Read the existing blog seed script (look for `prisma/seed-blog*.ts` and `lib/blog.ts` to match the exact post shape/fields) and ADD posts (new seed file like `prisma/seed-blog-updates.ts`, or extend the pattern) for: **Vibe coding — build sites & apps with no code on a VPS**, **Claude Code pre-installed on every Nxeon VPS**, **In-browser terminal — build straight from your server**, **Business email for domains registered anywhere (DNS setup guide)**, **How to migrate to Nxeon for free**, and 2–3 more tied to real features (game server customization, free SSL, block storage). Real, useful, 600–1000+ words each, with unique titles/slugs/descriptions/keywords matching the existing posts' schema. Make the seed script idempotent (upsert by slug) and runnable via `npx tsx`. Do NOT run it against the DB — just create it; the parent seeds/deploys.
5. Update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`: append a concise entry describing ONLY the SEO fixes + new blog posts you made (don't document things you didn't do).

Verify: `cd /opt/nxeon && npx tsc --noEmit 2>&1 | grep -v "test/.*test.ts"` clean and `npm run build` exits 0. Report: the title/og fix approach, how many pages you touched, the new blog slugs, and confirm og:title now varies per page.

33	## What WHOIS actually queries
34	
35	When a domain is registered, the registrar publishes a record to a **WHOIS server** run by the registry that manages that top-level domain (Verisign for \`.com\`, for example). 37	## Reading a WHOIS record field by field
38	
39	A typical record looks intimidating, but only a handful of fields matter most of the time.
40	
41	- **Domain Name** — the domain itself, normalised to uppercase.
42	- **Registrar** — the company you'd buy or transfer the domain through (GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare, and so on). If you want to contact the current owner, the registrar is your route.
43	- **Creation Date / Registered On** — when the domain was first registered. A domain created fifteen years ago carries more trust than one registered last week.
44	- **Registry Expiry Date** — when the registration lapses if not renewed. This is the field to watch if you're hoping to catch a dropping domain, or making sure your own doesn't expire.
45	- **Updated Date** — the last time the record changed. A recent update can signal a transfer or a name-server change.

60

473	
474	## An IP address is two parts
475	
476	An IPv4 address like \`192.168.1.10\` is 32 bits, written as four 8-bit **octets** (0–255 each). A subnet splits those 32 bits into two sections:
477	
478	- A **network** portion — identifies the network everyone on it shares.
479	- A **host** portion — identifies the individual device within that network.
480	
481	The **subnet mask** is what draws the line between them. Everything to the left of the line is network; everything to the right is host.
482	
483	## CIDR notation: the /number
484	
485	**CIDR** (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) writes the mask as a slash and a count of network bits:
486	
487	- \`/24\` means the first 24 bits are network, leaving 8 bits for hosts.
488	- \`/16\` means 16 network bits, 16 host bits.
489	- \`/8\` means 8 network bits, 24 host bits.
490	
491	So \`192.168.1.0/24\` is a network where the first three octets are fixed and the last octet varies per host. That's the most common home/office network you'll see.

495	The mask is just those network bits set to 1, written in dotted-decimal:
496

502	| /27 | 255.255.255.224 | 5 | 32 | 30 |

507

966	
967	Your MX records are completely independent of your website's A record, which is why you can host your site on your VPS and your email with a provider like Google Workspace or Fastmail at the same time.
968	
969	## The deliverability trio: SPF, DKIM, DMARC
970	
971	Receiving your mail is one thing; getting *your outbound* mail trusted is another. Spammers forge sender addresses constantly, so mailbox providers won't trust a domain that hasn't proven which servers may send for it. Three TXT-based records do that proving.
972	
973	### SPF — who is allowed to send
974	
975	**SPF (Sender Policy Framework)** is a TXT record listing the servers permitted to send mail as your domain:
976	
977	\`\`\`
978	example.com.    TXT    "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:mail.example.com ~all"
979	\`\`\`
980	
981	- \`include:\` pulls in a provider's authorised servers.
982	- \`~all\` means "anything else is suspicious (soft fail)"; \`-all\` means "reject anything else (hard fail)."
983	
984	If you send from Google Workspace, your VPS, and a newsletter tool, **all three** must appear in SPF or their mail may be flagged. A common mistake is having more than one SPF record — you're only allowed one; merge them.
985	
986	### DKIM — a cryptographic signature
987	
988	**DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)** signs each outgoing message with a private key; the matching public key lives in a TXT record at a selector subdomain:
989	
990	\`\`\`
991	selector._domainkey.example.com.    TXT    "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIGfMA0G..."
992	\`\`\`
993	
994	The receiver fetches the public key, verifies the signature, and confirms the message wasn't forged or altered in transit. Your mail provider generates the key and tells you the exact record to publish.
995	
996	### DMARC — the policy that ties it together
997	
998	**DMARC** tells receivers what to do when a message fails SPF and DKIM, and where to send reports:
999	
1000	\`\`\`
1001	_dmarc.example.com.    TXT    "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com"
1002	\`\`\`
1003	
1004	- \`p=none\` — monitor only (start here to see reports without affecting delivery).
1005	- \`p=quarantine\` — send failing mail to spam.
1006	- \`p=reject\` — refuse failing mail outright (the strongest, once you're confident).
1007	- \`rua=\` — the address that receives aggregate reports, so you can see who's sending as your domain.
1008	
1009	Best practice is to launch with \`p=none\`, read the reports for a couple of weeks to confirm all your legitimate senders pass, then tighten to \`quarantine\` and eventually \`reject\`.

    publishedAt: new Date("2026-07-17"),
    body: `A professional address like \`you@yourbusiness.com\` builds instant trust — but here's the part people miss: **your domain doesn't have to be registered with your email provider to use it.** Email routing is controlled entirely by DNS records, and DNS can be pointed from any registrar to any mail host. So whether your domain lives at Namecheap, GoDaddy, Cloudflare or anywhere else, you can run Nxeon business email on it by adding a handful of records. Here's exactly how.

## The key idea: DNS decides where mail goes

Two things about a domain are separate and often confused:

- **Where the domain is registered** — the registrar you pay to own the name.
- **Where the domain's DNS is hosted** — whoever answers DNS queries for it (often the registrar, sometimes a separate provider like Cloudflare).

Email delivery is governed by **DNS records**, not by the registrar. When someone emails you, their server looks up your domain's **MX records** and delivers to whatever host those point at. Change the MX records to point at your mail provider and mail flows there — no domain transfer required. This is why "registered anywhere" works.

## Step 1: Find where your DNS is managed

Before adding records, know where to add them. Your domain's **name servers** (NS records) determine who controls its DNS. If you never changed them, that's usually your registrar's DNS panel. If you set the domain up on Cloudflare or another DNS host, that's where records must go — editing them at the registrar will do nothing. A quick WHOIS or DNS lookup shows the current name servers if you're unsure.

## Step 2: Add the MX records

MX (Mail Exchange) records tell the world which servers accept mail for your domain. In your DNS host's panel, add the MX records your provider specifies. They look like:

\`\`\`
Type: MX   Name: @   Priority: 10   Value: mail.yourprovider.example.
Type: MX   Name: @   Priority: 20   Value: mail2.yourprovider.example.
\`\`\`

- **Name \`@\`** means the root domain (\`yourbusiness.com\`).
- **Priority** — lower numbers are tried first; the second is a fallback.
- The value is a **hostname, not an IP**, and it must end where your provider tells you.

Remove any old MX records left over from a previous mail setup — stray MX records cause mail to split or vanish.

## Step 3: Add SPF (who may send as you)

SPF is a **TXT record** listing the servers allowed to send mail for your domain. It stops spammers forging your address and keeps your legitimate mail out of spam:

\`\`\`
Type: TXT   Name: @   Value: "v=spf1 include:_spf.yourprovider.example ~all"
\`\`\`

Two rules that trip people up:

- You may have **only one** SPF record. If you already send from another service (a newsletter tool, say), merge both \`include:\` entries into a single record rather than adding a second.
- \`~all\` means "anything else is suspicious"; \`-all\` is stricter ("reject anything else"). Start with \`~all\`.

## Step 4: Add DKIM (a cryptographic signature)

DKIM signs your outgoing mail so receivers can confirm it wasn't forged or altered. Your provider generates a key and gives you a TXT record to publish at a **selector** subdomain:

\`\`\`
Type: TXT   Name: selector._domainkey   Value: "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIGfMA0G..."
\`\`\`

Copy the record exactly as provided — the long key string is unforgiving of stray spaces or line breaks. Once published, receivers fetch the public key, verify the signature, and trust the message.

## Step 5: Add DMARC (the policy that ties it together)

DMARC tells receiving servers what to do when a message fails SPF and DKIM, and where to send reports:

\`\`\`
Type: TXT   Name: _dmarc   Value: "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourbusiness.com"
\`\`\`

- **\`p=none\`** — monitor only. Start here so you can read reports without affecting delivery.

Launch at \`p=none\`, watch the reports for a week or two to confirm all your real mail passes, then tighten to \`quarantine\` and eventually \`reject\`.

DNS changes propagate over the record's **TTL** — usually minutes, occasionally a couple of hours. Don't panic if mail doesn't flow instantly. When it's had time to settle, confirm the records took effect with a DNS lookup: check that your **MX** points at your provider and that your **SPF, DKIM and DMARC** TXT records are live. Here's what block storage is, when to reach for it, and how to attach and mount a volume on Linux.

## What block storage actually is

A **block-storage volume** is a virtual disk you can attach to a server, separate from the server's built-in OS disk. To the operating system it looks and behaves like a physical drive: you format it, mount it, and read and write files to it as usual. But it's decoupled from the VPS — you can detach it, keep it, and reattach it elsewhere.

On Nxeon, volumes are **NVMe-backed**, so the extra capacity is fast, not a slow bulk tier. You get performance and room at the same time, billed simply at a flat per-GB monthly rate for what you provision.

## Block storage vs resizing the server

Both give you more disk, but they solve different problems:

- **Resizing the VPS** grows the base plan — usually vCPU, RAM *and* disk together. Use it when you need more *compute*, not just space.
- **A block-storage volume** adds *only* storage, independently, and can be attached, detached and moved. Use it when your CPU and RAM are fine but you're running out of room.

If your server is fast enough but the disk is filling, a volume is the cheaper, cleaner answer than paying for a bigger plan you don't otherwise need.

## When a volume is the right choice

- **Databases that keep growing.** Put the data directory on a volume so it can expand without resizing the whole box.
- **User uploads and media.** Images, video and documents pile up; a volume keeps them off the OS disk.
- **Backups and archives.** Store local backups on separate storage so a full OS disk never takes down the server.
- **Data you want to outlive the server.** Because a volume survives detachment, you can destroy and rebuild the VPS while keeping the data intact on the volume.
- **Portable datasets.** Move a volume between servers to shift a large dataset without copying it over the network.

## A key benefit: your data survives detach

This is the feature people underrate. A block-storage volume is **independent of the server's lifecycle**. Rebuild the VPS, reinstall the OS, or migrate to a new server, and the volume — with all its data — is still there to reattach. Your important data lives on storage that isn't tied to any one server instance, and the OS disk stays protected because your growing data isn't crammed onto it.

## How to attach and mount a volume

The workflow on Nxeon takes three steps: create, attach, mount.

**1. Create the volume** in your dashboard, choosing the size you need (you're billed per GB for what you provision).

**2. Attach it to your VPS.** It appears in the server as a new block device, typically something like \`/dev/sdb\` or \`/dev/vdb\`. Confirm which:

\`\`\`
lsblk
\`\`\`

Look for the new, unmounted device at the size you created.

**3. Format it (first time only).** A brand-new volume has no filesystem. Create one — ext4 is a safe default:

\`\`\`
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb
\`\`\`

Only do this on a *new* volume — formatting erases data, so never run it on a volume that already holds files.

**4. Mount it.** Make a mount point and mount the volume there:

\`\`\`
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data
sudo mount /dev/sdb /mnt/data
\`\`\`

Your extra space is now available at \`/mnt/data\`.

**5. Mount it automatically on boot.** So it comes back after a reboot, add it to \`/etc/fstab\`. Use the volume's UUID rather than the device name, which can change:

\`\`\`

# then add a line to /etc/fstab using the UUID, e.g.:
# UUID=xxxx-xxxx  /mnt/data  ext4  defaults,nofail  0  2
\`\`\`

The \`nofail\` option means the server still boots even if the volume is ever detached — a sensible safety net.

Once mounted, point your application at it. For a database, that means moving the data directory to the volume and updating the config to use the new path; for uploads, storing them under the mount point. Stop the service, move the data, update the path, restart — and from then on your growing data lands on the volume, keeping the OS disk lean.

All work is complete and verified. Here's the summary.

## Report

### Title/OG fix approach

**Bug 1 — doubled title suffix** (`app/layout.tsx`): the root `title.template` was `"%s · Nxeon"` while every page's `metadata.title` already ended in `— Nxeon`/`| Nxeon`, rendering e.g. `"VPS Hosting — Nxeon · Nxeon"`. Fixed by (a) changing the template to `"%s — Nxeon"` (homepage keeps its full `title.default`, no template), and (b) stripping the trailing suffix from every page's `metadata.title`. Verified in built HTML: `<title>VPS Hosting — Nxeon</title>`, `About — Nxeon`, etc. — exactly one suffix.

**Bug 2 — identical og:title/og:description everywhere**: the root layout hardcoded `openGraph.title`/`description` (and `twitter.title`/`description`) as plain strings, so every page inherited the same social preview. I **removed** those root-level title/description defaults (keeping `type`/`siteName`/`url`/`locale` + twitter `card`). With no root default, Next.js 15 infers `og:title`/`twitter:title` from each page's resolved `<title>` (so they carry the single `— Nxeon` suffix) and `og:description`/`twitter:description` from each page's `description`. Confirmed by curling built HTML — og:title now varies per page (`About — Nxeon`, `Features — Nxeon`, `Block Storage — Nxeon`, `Compare Nxeon — honest VPS comparisons`, …) and og:description matches each page's own description.

Note: a template object on the root og.title (the originally-suggested approach) does **not** work here — I tested it and pages without their own og.title fell back to the root default. Removing the defaults so Next infers per-page is what actually makes them vary.

Pages that set their own `openGraph.title` (blog, help, status, compare, vps-vs-*, game-servers, tools) keep it. The two whose custom og title lacked the brand after stripping (game-servers, tools) had `— Nxeon` restored so every og:title stays branded.
